meta.name: ABACBS 2026
meta.venue: Storey Hall (Building 16), RMIT University City Campus
meta.note: Provisional program — subject to change. Built from the official ABACBS 2026 combined program (PDF) and the program spreadsheet dated 17 Oct 2026.

info.getting_here: Trains: Melbourne Central or State Library stations. Trams: Swanston St stop 7/8, La Trobe St stop 6 (Free Tram Zone). No conference parking — public transport recommended.
info.registration_desk: Level 2, immediately upon entering the building. ABACBS volunteers welcome you at the Swanston Street entrance.
info.posters: Back of Storey Hall Auditorium (L5) and the Green Brain Room (L7). Odd numbers at morning tea, even numbers at afternoon tea (Tue & Wed). A0 portrait.
info.social: Official hashtag #ABACBS2026. Primary platform is BlueSky (@abacbs.bsky.social); there is also the ABACBS Slack.
info.access: Venue is wheelchair accessible with lifts. Smoking and vaping are not permitted anywhere on RMIT campus. Accessibility or carer needs: conference@abacbs.org.

events.title: SBEI 2026 — Symposium on Bioinformatics and Engineered Intelligence
events.room: Lecture Theatre, Level 1, Building 16 (336–348 Swanston St)
events.desc: Run by the ABACBS professional subcommittee, focused on GenAI across AgTech, Biotech and HealthTech. Registration from 8:15am, opening address 8:50am, close 5:30pm. Keynotes: Prof. Daniel MacArthur (Garvan / MCRI) and Prof. Michael Stumpf (University of Melbourne / Cell Bauhaus). Sessions: Population-Scale Bioinformatics (Lyn Griffiths, Jimmy Breen, Adam Heterick, Jeff Christiansen); Clinical Genomics in Practice (Simon Sadedin, Lynn Fink, Eva Chan, Claire Lillee); Applied & Environmental Bioinformatics (Mathew Lewsey, Clare Sloggett, Monica Nolan, Matthew Andrews); Bioinformatics Engineering (Allan Leung, James Bradley, Gregg Bass, Anna Quaglieri).

events.title: COMBINE Symposium 2026
events.desc: Annual symposium of COMBINE, the Australian computational biology and bioinformatics student society. Student research talks, workshops and networking.

events.title: ABACBS EMCR Funding Futures
events.desc: EMCR Funding Futures event. Three $500 travel scholarships are available for postdocs — apply via the EMCR-2026 page.

workshops.title: Multi-task single-cell omics: integration, benchmarking, and condition-aware inference
workshops.audience: The workshop is intended for bioinformaticians, computational biologists, data scientists and researchers who analyse or plan to analyse multimodal, multi-batch or multi-condition single-cell data. It is suitable for postgraduate students, postdoctoral researc
workshops.prereq: Participants should have basic familiarity with single-cell data analysis and common concepts such as cell types, batches, dimensionality reduction, and train/test evaluation. Basic Python and Jupyter Notebook experience is recommended; advanced programming or
workshops.abstract:
Multimodal single-cell datasets increasingly combine transcriptomic, protein, and chromatin measurements across batches, conditions, and patients. Analysts must select an integration strategy suited to their study design, assess whether biological information is preserved, and obtain interpretable cell- and patient-level results without removing condition-associated signals.

This hands-on workshop presents a task-centred workflow using three open-source tools. Participants will use scMultiBench to distinguish vertical, diagonal, mosaic and cross-modality integration settings (defined by how cells, features and modalities are shared across datasets) and compare methods using task-specific measures of batch correction, biological conservation, classification, imputation and computational efficiency. They will then use Matilda to learn a shared multimodal representation for data augmentation, cell type classification, dimension reduction, and feature selection. Finally, they will use M3 for condition-aware integration, donor-level prediction and interpretation at gene, cell, and cell-type resolutions.

By the end, participants will be able to: (1) match multimodal study designs to ap

workshops.title: Modelling continuous cell states using scRNA-seq data
workshops.audience: Researchers and students who analyse scRNA-seq data and want to move beyond discrete cell types to model continuous processes such as development, differentiation, activation and disease progression.
workshops.abstract:
Many biological processes are continuous, and they should be modelled continuously. In his workshop, we will introduce statistical approaches for modelling continuous cell states from scRNA-seq data.

Using data from human heart development as an example, participants will follow a workflow across three modules of analysis. First, they will use Φ-Space to enrich discrete cell labels with continuous phenotype scores learned from a reference. Second, they will infer cardiomyocyte maturation trajectories using slingshot and diffusion pseudotime, and compare inferred trajectories using different cell embeddings. Third, they will use NeighbourNet to investigate how cell-specific co-expression patterns vary along the maturation continuum.

We will start the workshop with a short conceptual presentation, followed by guided practical expercises and interpretation of model outputs. We will keep the emphasis on modelling choices and biological interpretation.

By the end of this work, participants will be able to identify when continuous modelling is appropriate; construct and interpret cell phenotype scores; fit, visualise and critically compare pseudotime inference methods; explore cell-sp

workshops.title: Transcripts, Embeddings, and Niches: A Practical Guide to Graph Neural Networks in Spatial Transcriptomics
workshops.audience: Bioinformaticians and biologists who are interested in analysing imaged-based spatial transcriptomics data
workshops.prereq: Basic familiarity with R/Python and Unix command line
workshops.abstract:
Image-based spatial transcriptomics (iST) now resolve tissue architecture at single-transcript resolution, but analyses are still limited. Segmentation introduces ambiguity to data due to unreliable cell borders, overlapping cells, or transcript noise. Additionally, most tools for ST analysis struggle when being scaled to large cohorts. 

In this workshop, we present a new Snakemake workflow designed for segmentation-free, highly scalable analysis of iST data. The workflow applies Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) directly on transcript-level data, bypassing the cell segmentation step entirely, and produces common analysis endpoints such as spatial domains and differential gene expression analyses. 

Through a hands-on session, participants will learn how to generate molecular graphs from tissue samples, as well as methods to visualise and interpret outputs in biological contexts such as spatial niche detection and tissue architecture characterisation. By the end of the workshop, attendees will be equipped to apply this segmentation-free workflow to their own spatial transcriptomics datasets, enabling reproducible, transcript-level insights into complex tissue biology without the errors

workshops.title: Omnibenchmark: orchestrating transparent, reproducible, extensible and standardized scientific benchmarks
workshops.audience: This workshop would be relevant to all computational biologists and especially method users and developers, since benchmarks represent the evidence we gather to demonstrate the merit of computational methods.
workshops.prereq:
Unix command line expertise is essential; some bash scripting knowledge would be helpful.
Basic familiarity with R/Python and with the conda package manager would be helpful. 
Basic familiarity with git/github would also be recommended.
workshops.abstract: Computational biology benchmarks, separate from "challenges", are formal scientific comparisons of computational methods, accompanied by a collection of independently useful artifacts (e.g., software environments, data, code, etc.). The aim of a benchmark is to offer a review of the developments for a well-defined computational task by summarizing the available methods and their strengths. Importantly, identifying a single best method is not the ultimate goal; instead, the goal is to arrive at a set of performant methods across a plurality of datasets for a subtask. Benchmarks draw on a range of (sometimes domain-specific) techniques, including the generation of synthetic datasets that mimic real data or the use of ground truth derived from real experimental data or from biology; notably, producing appropriate reference datasets is resource intensive. Performance criteria are then defined for the task at hand (the importance of which can differ across researchers) and methods are evaluated; in some cases, relevant criteria may need to be developed as new understanding of data and methods emerges. This hands-on workshop is designed for and relevant to all computational biologists, s

workshops.title: From Reads to Isoforms: Long-Read RNA-Seq Analysis with bambu across Bulk, Single-Cell and Spatial Data
workshops.audience:
This workshop is aimed at researchers who are already working with long-read RNA sequencing data or planning to do so, whether bulk, single-cell or spatial, and more broadly at anyone with a particular interest in long-read transcriptomic analysis.

workshops.prereq:
Assumed knowledge
Comfortable working in R, and familiar with basic RNA-seq concepts such as alignment, count matrices and differential expression.
No prior experience with bambu or other long-read tools is required, and no command-line experience: the worksho
workshops.abstract:
Long-read RNA sequencing resolves full-length transcripts, exposing the isoform diversity that shapes cellular identity and disease biology and that increasingly guides the design of RNA therapeutics. As these data become routine across bulk, single-cell and spatial protocols, the ability to analyse them reliably becomes more important. bambu, a Bioconductor R package for transcript discovery and quantification, is among the leading tools developed for this purpose, widely used in long-read studies and evaluated in independent benchmarks of long-read transcript analysis.

This 1.5-hour workshop demonstrates the use of bambu on bulk, single-cell and spatial long-read RNA sequencing data. The workshop starts with a 20-minute introduction covering state-of-the-art long-read sequencing technologies, the analytical challenges specific to single-cell and spatial long-read data, and how bambu addresses them. In the first hands-on session (30 minutes), participants run a complete bambu workflow on publicly available SG-NEx data, perform reference-guided transcript discovery and quantification, and learn how to interpret and tune the key outputs. The second hands-on session (30 minutes) cov

workshops.title: Spatial Taster – A quick sampler of spatial transcriptomics tests
workshops.audience: No spatial transcriptomics analysis experience is necessary, this workshop is aimed at those interested in understanding how it can be applied to testing biological hypotheses.  As a short workshop, it provides a brief introduction to what’s possible.
workshops.prereq: This workshop assumes basic knowledge of R.
workshops.abstract:
This workshop provides a practical introduction to comparative analysis of spatial omics data. Starting with a pre-processed in situ spatial dataset, we will undertake some basic differential expression, look at differences of proportions of cell types, and exploratory plotting. We will work in R, using mostly Bioconductor tools. We will use a cosMx dataset, but these approaches are applicable to other technologies like Xenium or vizgen.
Along the way we will discuss considerations specific to spatial analyses, how to scale it up to a full analysis, and how to assess our results. We will also introduce the Spatial Sampler collection of worked examples and code snippets for analyses on spatial datasets.

workshops.title: Vibe-sciencing, carefully: getting real analyses out of coding agents
workshops.audience:
Researchers who do their own computational analysis — PhD students, postdocs, staff bioinformaticians, and PIs.

Part 1 is for those who have heard about coding agents but have not used one, or have tried once and bounced off. Part 2 is for those who have used
workshops.prereq: Essential, both parts — a paid account or API credits. Every participant must arrive with an agentic coding tool installed, authenticated, and backed by a paid subscription or API credits. This is not optional: free tiers rate-limit within minutes of hands-on
workshops.abstract:
Coding agents have moved quickly from novelty to daily tool for many computational biologists. Used well, they compress the distance between a biological question and a working analysis. Used carelessly, they produce plausible-looking pipelines that are subtly wrong and hard to audit. This workshop runs as two independent 90-minute sessions; participants may attend either or both.

Part 1 — Getting started with coding assistants. For people who have not used one. We install and configure an agent, connect it to a real project, and work through a small coding example together: how a session is structured, what the agent can and cannot see, how to give it context through project files such as CLAUDE.md, how permissions and tool access work, and how to keep the whole thing inside a reproducible environment and under version control. We also cover a few tips on getting the most out of your tokens. The emphasis is on establishing habits — small verifiable steps, everything in git — before speed becomes tempting.

Part 2 — Vibe-sciencing in practice. For people who have used coding assistants already, but not yet for data analysis. We work through some case studies exploring the possibil

workshops.title: Taxonomic profiling and MAG building from long-read metagenomics
workshops.audience: Researchers and students who work with, or are about to start working with, microbial community sequencing data, and who want to use long reads effectively.
workshops.prereq:
Comfort with the Unix command line is essential.

Basic familiarity with sequencing data concepts (FASTQ, contigs, coverage, taxonomy). Prior metagenomics experience is helpful but not required.

A laptop with a modern web browser, a terminal, and a working SS
workshops.abstract:
Long-read sequencing is quickly becoming a mainstream option for metagenomics. Both Oxford Nanopore (R10.4.1 and later) and PacBio HiFi now deliver accuracy sufficient for routine metagenome assembly, and long reads regularly yield complete, circularised genomes from complex communities. This hands-on workshop covers the practical analysis of long-read metagenomes end to end.

Participants will work through a realistic dataset. We will begin with quality control and a look at how modern long-read error profiles differ from short-read data and from earlier nanopore chemistries. We then cover read-based taxonomic profiling using single-copy marker genes, and how to estimate what fraction of a sample is prokaryotic, and why profiling and assembly can disagree. The second half moves to assembly with metaFlye, polishing with short-reads, binning of long-read assemblies, dereplication, and quality assessment and taxonomic assignment of the resulting MAGs.

By the end, participants will be able to run a complete long-read metagenomics analysis.

workshops.title: ATAClone: Cancer Clone Identification and Copy Number Estimation from Single-cell ATAC-seq
workshops.audience:
Recommended for those interested in the following topics:
10X scATAC-seq or scRNA-seq + scATAC-seq studies of cancer
Single-cell copy number estimation
Normalisation and clustering of single-cell data
workshops.prereq:
Basic familiarity with R
Installation of the ATAClone package from our Github (https://github.com/TrigosTeam/ATAClone) if working on a personal device
workshops.abstract:
Single-cell analyses of cancer typically begin by identifying distinct populations of cancer cells by unsupervised clustering. However, in many cases this clustering is explained simply by differences in the copy number. To detect and estimate these differences in copy number, we have developed ATAClone. Applicable to both standalone and multiome scATAC-seq assays, ATAClone first identifies cancer ‘clones’ with shared copy number profiles, then estimates the copy number of each clone jointly. Advantages over other single-cell copy number calling tools include completely automated clone identification as well as ploidy-aware copy number estimation. 

In this workshop, participants will be guided through all key steps of a typical ATAClone workflow. These steps include selection of a set of 'stably-accessible' regions for which copy number signal is maximised,  automated filtering of 10X single-cell RNA-seq + ATAC-seq data for high quality cells, application of a variance-stabilising transformation and PCA to separate clones by their copy number differences, optimisation of the Leiden algorithm to minimise false positive clones, and derivation of absolute copy number based on total D

workshops.title: From Reads to Resistance: An End-to-End Antimicrobial Resistance Analysis with BV-BRC
workshops.audience: The workshop is intended for graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, bioinformaticians, computational biologists, microbiologists, clinical infectious-disease and antimicrobial-resistance researchers, genomic epidemiologists, and others interested in appl
workshops.prereq:
Participants should have a basic understanding of molecular biology, microbiology, or genomics. No programming or command-line experience is required.

Participants must:

• Bring a laptop with a modern web browser.
• Register for a free BV-BRC account before
workshops.abstract:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health challenge and an important application of high-throughput sequencing, microbial genomics, and metagenomics. Translating sequence data into an understanding of resistance often requires integrating multiple computational analyses spanning genome reconstruction, annotation, comparative genomics, sequence variation, protein structure, and phylogenetics.

This full-day, hands-on workshop will guide participants through an end-to-end investigation of AMR using the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), a freely available bioinformatics platform for infectious-disease research.

Working with real sequencing datasets, participants will assess the quality and taxonomic composition of metagenomic reads, identify AMR genes through read mapping, and reconstruct individual bacterial genomes through metagenomic binning. Participants will then annotate genomes and compare resistant and susceptible isolates to investigate the genomic basis of resistance. The investigation will progress from genomes to genes and proteins: participants will identify resistance-associated sequence variation, examine variants in three-dimen

workshops.title: blisa: Inferring Cell–Cell Communication from Spatial Transcriptomics
workshops.audience: This workshop is aimed at researchers and bioinformaticians working with or planning to work with spatial transcriptomics data, who want to add cell–cell communication analysis to their toolkit.
workshops.prereq: Basic familiarity with R
workshops.abstract:
Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatial context that can improve the inference of cell–cell communication (CCC), but analysing CCC from spatial data presents challenges including sparse imaging-based ST (iST) measurements, appropriate definition of spatial neighbourhoods, and computational scalability.

This hands-on workshop will introduce blisa, an R package that infers CCC from ST data using Bivariate Local Moran’s I statistics. blisa works on both imaging-based (e.g. Xenium) and sequencing-based (e.g. Visium) ST. It aggregates cell-level data into hexagonal bins to reduce sparsity and computational cost while preserving local spatial structure, identifies hotspots where ligand and receptor expression co-localise, and summarises signalling at the pathway and cell-type level.

Working through real Xenium and Visium datasets, participants build a complete workflow: preparing and binning spatial data, curating ligand–receptor pairs, detecting hotspots with permutation-based significance testing, quantifying sender–receiver relationships between cell types, and producing spatial maps and heatmaps. We also cover platform-specific pitfalls, e.g., detection sensitivity that shape

workshops.title: Differential transcript expression and differential transcript usage using Salmon and edgeR
workshops.audience: People who are interested in transcript-level RNA-seq analysis
workshops.prereq: basic familiarity with R and Unix command line; pre-installation of R (version 4.5.2 or later) and required R packages (edgeR version 4.8.2, limma version 3.66.0, rtracklayer version 1.70.1, ggplot2 version 4.0.2, Gviz version 1.54.0, pheatmap version 1.0.13,
workshops.abstract:
Differential transcript expression (DTE) and differential transcript usage (DTU) analyses provide high-resolution insights into transcript-level changes and regulatory mechanisms. In this hands-on workshop, participants will learn an end-to-end workflow for transcript-level RNA-seq analysis using Salmon and the recently developed edgeR DTE and DTU frameworks. These frameworks incorporate quantification-uncertainty correction and new quasi-likelihood methods, offering strong statistical power, false discovery rate control and computational efficiency.

Using RNA-seq data from human lung adenocarcinoma cell lines and the complete telomere-to-telomere human reference genome (T2T-CHM13), participants will learn to quantify transcript abundance with Salmon, organise GFF-based transcript annotations, and assess DTE and DTU with edgeR while accounting for read-to-transcript ambiguity and biological variation. Although demonstrated using the human T2T-CHM13 reference, the workflow can be applied to any well-annotated reference transcriptome.

By the end of the workshop, participants will be able to conduct and interpret robust transcript-level analyses across diverse organisms and referenc

workshops.title: Hello nf-core – Intermediate Nextflow training
workshops.audience: researchers and bioinformaticians who have had some contact with Nextflow/workflow managers, maybe have written a basic pipeline, and want to take their skills to their next level.
workshops.prereq: Must know basic Nextflow, at a minimum complete the Hello Nextflow training: https://training.nextflow.io/2.8.1/hello_nextflow/
workshops.abstract:
This workshop uses official Nextflow training material. Here is the description taken directly from their website:

This course is designed to be hands-on, with goal-oriented exercises structured to introduce information gradually.

You will be introduced to nf-core, a community effort to develop and maintain a curated set of scientific pipelines built using Nextflow, as well as relevant tooling and guidelines that promote open development, testing, and peer review (Nat Biotechnol 38, 276–278 (2020), Genome Biol 26, 228 (2025)).

The pipelines developed by the nf-core community are designed to be modular, scalable, and portable, allowing researchers to easily adapt and execute them using their own data and compute resources. The best practices guidelines enforced by the project further ensure that the pipelines are robust, well-documented, and validated against real-world datasets. This helps to increase the reliability and reproducibility of scientific analyses and ultimately enables researchers to accelerate their scientific discoveries.

We won't cover everything there is to know about nf-core pipelines in this course, because nf-core encompasses many features and conventions de

workshops.title: Work less, garden more: Quick wins for scientific computing
workshops.audience: Novices to large scale data analysis; Practising bioinformaticians that would like to improve their computational throughput
workshops.prereq: Experience with the terminal / command prompt is desirable.
workshops.abstract:
This practical workshop will improve bioinformaticians’ ability to get their science done faster. Too often, scientific outputs are delayed by computational bottlenecks that could be avoided with some minor tweaks. We will present core optimisation techniques, distilled into practical takeaways that attendees can implement same-day. Key topics include:

- Easy ways to gain speedups with parallelism
- Avoiding I/O slowdowns
- Advanced UNIX command line tips and tricks
- Picking the right compute infrastructure for the job
- Faster data transfers
- Sleuthing where the bottlenecks are 

The workshop is designed to be infrastructure-agnostic, spanning laptop, cloud, and HPC. Attendees will gain understanding of HPC scheduling and cloud-native approaches such as queue-based workflows and serverless computing, enabling participants to match infrastructure choices to the scale and complexity of their analyses. We will also outline how to obtain access to Australian research computing resources, and outline how to benchmark your code for national compute grant schemes. We will provide guidance on how and when to ask for help, which is a common area of uncertainty.

workshops.title: cellNexus and sccomp: From the Human Cell Atlas to insights
workshops.prereq: Prior experience with single-cell analyses or linear models is beneficial but not necessary.
workshops.abstract:
The Human Cell Atlas and CELLxGENE now host hundreds of millions of harmonised single cells spanning healthy and diseased tissues. This data availability created enormous opportunities to unveil biological mechanisms at high resolution across cell types, tissues and population niches. However, identifying a collection of atlases is only a small part of the effort. Making large-scale data analysis ready requires weeks or months of work.
This hands-on workshop introduces cellNexus, an API for R and Python that delivers quality control, annotation, and analysis layers for CELLxGENE-scale single-cell data. It allows you to conveniently create ready-to-use SingleCellExperiment and/or Seurat objects of arbitrary selections of cells. Beyond expression data, cellNexus also standardises cell type labels across studies through multi-reference consensus annotation and enriches samples with standardised metadata, including age, ethnicity, and tissue groups. This enhanced metadata supports large-scale modelling, for example of cell-type composition patterns. workshops.title: Introduction to imaging-based spatial transcriptomics analysis
workshops.audience: This workshop will be relevant to anyone interested in analysing data from emerging high-resolution imaging-based spatial molecular technologies such as 10x Xenium, NanoString CosMx, and Vizgen MERSCOPE.
workshops.prereq: Attendees will require a laptop with internet access and should have familiarity with R and/or python, some familiarity with Bioconductor and/or with deploying jupyter notebooks. Some basic knowledge on spatial transcriptomics technologies and the standard ste
workshops.abstract:
This hands-on workshop provides a practical introduction to bioinformatics analysis of high-resolution spatial transcriptomics data, with a focus on extracting biologically meaningful signals from complex tissue environments. Using a representative spatial transcriptomics dataset, participants will work through key steps from data quality control to spatial differential expression and feature selection.

Participants will learn to:
•	Perform quality control and spatial normalisation (SpaNorm) of spatial transcriptomics data
•	Conduct basic cell typing and clustering to characterise cellular populations and spatial organisation
•	Identify spatially variable and differentially expressed features, including continuous spatial differential expression using spiDE
•	Perform feature selection using modern methods such as Stabl and traditional covariate-adjusted approaches, including linear elastic net models
•	Identify spatially-aware marker genes and perform gene set testing with JazzPanda
•	Interpret spatial molecular patterns and integrate computational results to generate biological insights

workshops.title: From Raw Reads to Cancer Insights: Hands-on Long-Read Sequencing Analysis
workshops.audience:
This workshop is intended for bioinformaticians, computational biologists, cancer researchers, molecular scientists, clinical genomics researchers and postgraduate students who want to begin analysing long-read cancer sequencing data.

It will be particularly
workshops.prereq:
Participants should have:

Basic familiarity with genomic sequencing data and variant terminology.
Basic experience using the Unix command line.
Introductory experience with either R or Python.
A laptop with at least 8 GB RAM and approximately 10 GB of free st
workshops.abstract:
Long-read sequencing technologies provide an increasingly accessible way to investigate cancer genomes beyond the capabilities of conventional short-read sequencing. Individual reads can span complex structural variants, repetitive regions and phased alleles while simultaneously capturing native DNA methylation. However, integrating these signals into a reproducible cancer analysis workflow remains challenging for many researchers.

This hands-on workshop will introduce participants to the analysis and interpretation of Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing data in cancer genomics. Using a small, computationally manageable tumour–normal dataset, participants will follow the major stages of an analysis workflow, from assessing read and alignment quality to examining somatic single-nucleotide variants, structural variants, copy-number alterations, DNA methylation and haplotype-resolved events. Particular attention will be given to recognising common artefacts, evaluating read-level evidence and integrating different molecular signals to distinguish well-supported cancer-associated events from uncertain calls.

Practical exercises will use command-line tools and lightweight R or Python

workshops.title: Accelerate your Research with Cloud Computing on the ARDC Nectar Research Cloud
workshops.prereq: No cloud computing or coding experience is required to attend.
workshops.abstract:
Don't let limited computing power slow down your research. The ARDC Nectar Research Cloud provides fast and scalable computing resources tailored specifically for research.

Whether you need to run intensive data analyses and complex simulations, train AI and ML models, manage big data or collaborate seamlessly across institutions, Nectar gives you the computational power to scale up your work.

Join us for an interactive introduction to Nectar, where we'll cover:
-	 What is cloud computing and how can it accelerate my research?
-	 Real-world case studies powered by Nectar.
-	 Guidance on accessing tutorials and ongoing support.
-	 Live Q&A to answer your questions.

No cloud computing or coding experience is required to attend.

workshops.title: From Questions to Research Strategies: Scientific Brainstorming with AI Agents
workshops.audience: Computational biologists of any level with an introductory understanding of Python will be more autonomous to advance on the hands-on part of the workshop.
workshops.prereq:
Participants are expected to know how to prepare a Python environment in their personal computers.
Presenters can share in advance any requirements for the implementation of the Virtual Lab.

Even if participants choose not to bring a personal computer, the wa
workshops.abstract:
This hybrid walkthrough and hands-on workshop will introduce participants to the Virtual Lab, a recently developed multi-agent framework in which specialised AI agents collaborate through structured meetings to tackle scientific problems1. Instead of relying on a single assistant, the Virtual Lab orchestrates autonomous agents with complementary expertise that independently reason, critique one another's proposals, debate alternatives, and progressively design a research plan. Originally developed by James Zou and colleagues1, the framework provides a compelling example of how agentic AI can support scientific reasoning beyond conventional chatbot interactions.
This workshop will introduce the underlying architecture as a reusable framework for scientific brainstorming and research planning. Participants will learn how the Virtual Lab organises agents and how these run structured meetings, how prompts define individual expertise and responsibilities, how discussions are merged and framed as recommendations, and how iterative reasoning emerges from interactions between autonomous agents.

workshops.title: ELIXIR-GOBLET Train-the-Trainer: A Short-Course Introduction to Learner-Centred Training
workshops.audience:
This workshop is addressed to scientists:
- with some to little or no teaching experience,
- who want to become a teacher or a better one, and
- who believe teaching is - or may become - a relevant aspect of their professional development.
workshops.prereq: This workshop is designed for scientists with some to little or no teaching experience. No prior background in pedagogy is required.
workshops.abstract:
The ELIXIR-GOBLET Train-the-Trainer (TtT) course is the result of many years of collaboration among trainers, training coordinators, and training facilitators across the ELIXIR and GOBLET communities. Created in 2015, it has continued to evolve through the contributions, experience, and commitment of the ELIXIR-GOBLET TtT instructor community.

This 6-hour session offers a condensed introduction to the full 2-day TtT course, adapted for conference delegates who want a practical, evidence-based entry point into training design. Participants will explore key concepts from learning theory, instructional design, learner engagement, and feedback, and see how these concepts translate directly into everyday training situations.

The session supports a shift from a content-centred to a learner-centred approach to training. Rather than starting from what the trainer wants to present, participants will practise asking:

What should learners be able to do by the end of the training?
What learning experiences will help them get there?
How can we keep learners actively engaged?
How can we tell whether learning is actually happening?
How can feedback improve both learning and teaching?

workshops.title: Predictive Functional Genomics: Live-Coding with AlphaGenome and Bioconductor
workshops.audience: Computational Biologists with at least a basic understanding of the topic.
workshops.prereq: Being familiar with basic programming and, ideally, Google Colab and/or Python notebooks.
workshops.abstract:
Interpreting the functional consequences of genomic variants remains a central challenge in modern computational biology. This hands-on, 1.5-hour live-coding workshop introduces participants to AlphaGenome, a state-of-the-art deep learning model designed for sequence-to-function predictions. Attendees will explore how deep neural networks accurately forecast variant effects, gene expression, and regulatory dynamics directly from raw genomic sequence data.

In this fast-paced practical session, participants will execute live AlphaGenome queries to evaluate functional genomic variants across diverse regulatory contexts. To ensure maximum relevance for the BiocAsia community, the session focuses heavily on bridging Python-native deep learning frameworks with the R/Bioconductor ecosystem. Using packages such as reticulate, attendees will learn to seamlessly parse AlphaGenome’s prediction matrices directly into standard Bioconductor data containers, including GenomicRanges and SummarizedExperiment.
